summary: A is the preferable review candidate because it keeps file-specific logic localized and centralizes request handling, while B duplicates Files.Add and makes an explicitly out-of-scope global retry change. Neither patch fully satisfies the frozen contract.
reasons: A reuses multipartbody.NewFile and funnels Add and Upload through one private implementation, preserving a single location for options, request construction, decoding, and errors. B duplicates all of that logic inside Upload, contrary to the contract’s requirement to route through FilesService.Add.

B modifies RawClient.Do globally, changing retry, seeking, content-length, and reader-closing behavior for Raw().Do, Files.Add, Files.Update, and other seekable-body requests. The contract explicitly excludes unrelated retry refactoring and changes to Update.
B’s GetBody closure returns wrappers around the same mutable io.ReadSeeker rather than independent body copies, creating fragile behavior for redirects, retries, or any overlapping body use.

A’s tests directly verify the multipart field, filename, content, and complete multipart parsing on both attempts using an os.File source. B also verifies replay, but its multipart and retry assertions are split across tests and it adds substantial unrelated raw-client coverage.
risks_a: A improperly changes FilesService.Add to eagerly buffer every caller-provided body, altering streaming, memory use, blocking, and source-error timing despite the requirement to preserve Add behavior.
Upload calls the private add helper instead of FilesService.Add, so it misses the contract’s exact delegation requirement, even though the common behavior remains centralized.
The visible tests do not cover empty filename, nil content, or source-reader failures. Validation is left to multipartbody.NewFile rather than being explicit in Upload.
risks_b: Upload bypasses FilesService.Add and duplicates its option handling, request construction, response decoding, and error handling, inviting future divergence.
The raw-client changes are unnecessary for the buffered Upload implementation and violate scope discipline by changing seekable-body semantics SDK-wide, including Files.Update.

Seek-to-end can fail or have side effects for some io.ReadSeeker implementations, and returning the same seeker from GetBody does not honor the usual expectation of a fresh replay body reliably across all HTTP behaviors such as redirects or concurrent use contexts where body copies could overlap. The change also alters ownership by preventing the client from closing underlying seekable readers, which is outside the contract and may break existing expectations, while Add remains non-retryable for forward-only readers anyway, resulting in inconsistent semantics by reader type rather than preserving behavior uniformly. The visible tests cover validation but omit source-reader failures.
